prompt: Which description of a prompt matches what the model actually does with it?
hint: Lesson 1: what goes into the one step the model performs?

choices.text: The start of a text, which the model continues
choices.why: Right. The reply is the likeliest continuation of the text you gave it.

choices.text: An order that the model reads, understands and then carries out
choices.why: That picture explains the prompts that work and none of the ones that fail. The model continues text.

choices.text: A search query run against what the model has stored
choices.why: Nothing is looked up. The model scores the next piece of the text.

choices.text: A setting that chooses which of its answers to give
choices.why: There are no stored answers to choose between; there is a distribution over the next piece.

prompt: `the café opens at` gave `seven` and `eight`; `the café closes at` gave `six` and `noon`. What changed the prediction?
hint: Compare the two prompts word by word.

choices.text: An instruction to talk about closing time
choices.why: No instruction was given. The word `closes` was simply part of the text.

choices.text: A random seed that differed between the two runs
choices.why: `toylm next` prints the scores themselves; no draw was involved.

choices.text: The model having learnt something new about the café between the runs
choices.why: Nothing about the model changed. Only the text it was given did.

choices.text: One word of the text, `closes`
choices.why: Yes. The text is all the model has, so one word moved the whole distribution.

prompt: `question : when does the café open ? answer :` made `toylm` say `yes.` Why?
hint: Read the context line it printed.

choices.text: The model misread `when` as a yes-or-no question
choices.why: It never saw `when` at all. Its window was the last two words.

choices.text: There is no opening time anywhere in the corpus
choices.why: There is: `the café opens at seven` appears many times.

choices.text: Its window held only `answer :`, after which short replies like `yes` follow
choices.why: Right. The layout reached the model and the question did not: two words of window, lesson 1.

choices.text: Temperature 0 always picks the shortest word available
choices.why: Temperature 0 picks the highest score, which here was `yes` at 50%.

prompt: A large model would answer the `when does the café open` question properly. What does the `yes.` episode still teach about prompting one?
hint: Separate the window from the rule.

choices.text: Large models ignore layout and read only the words
choices.why: Layout is part of the text, and the text is all any model continues.

choices.text: It continues the shape of the text you give, not only its content
choices.why: Yes. A large model sees the whole question and still follows the language, register and format of the document.

choices.text: Question-and-answer layouts are forbidden in prompts and should be avoided
choices.why: Nothing forbids them. They steer the reply, which is useful when it is on purpose.

choices.text: Nothing; the episode shows a limit of `toylm` and does not transfer
choices.why: The window is `toylm`'s limit. Continuing the layout is what every model does.

prompt: In a chat API request, what does the model actually receive?

choices.text: Only the newest user message, with the rest of the chat kept on the provider's servers
choices.why: The application sends the whole conversation each time; the model has no memory between requests.

choices.text: The messages laid out as one text, ending inside an open assistant turn
choices.why: Right. Its reply is the continuation of that open turn.

choices.text: Each message separately, answered one by one and joined afterwards
choices.why: There is one text and one continuation.

choices.text: A summary of the conversation that the provider writes
choices.why: Nothing in the request is a summary unless a program wrote one.

prompt: An assistant seems to remember what you said ten messages ago. Where is that memory?
hint: Who sends what, on each request?

choices.text: In the request, resent each time
choices.why: Yes. The application sends the whole list again; the model itself keeps nothing between requests.

choices.text: In the model's weights, updated after each message you send to it
choices.why: Using a model does not train it. The weights are the same before and after your chat.

choices.text: In a database the model queries before every reply
choices.why: The model queries nothing. What it sees is the text of the request.

choices.text: In the system prompt, which the model rewrites as the chat goes on
choices.why: The system prompt is written by the developer and stays as written.

prompt: Match each role in a chat request to who writes it.

pairs.right: the model, one turn at a time

right_distractors: the provider of the model, once per day

prompt: The rules, the persona and the format an application sets for its assistant go in the message whose role is ___.
hint: The user does not see this one; lesson 22 is about it.

prompt: Which of these makes prompt writing engineering, in this lesson's sense?
hint: Five habits; what do they have in common?

choices.text: Knowing the phrases that unlock better answers
choices.why: Phrases are what you change. Engineering is how you find out whether the change helped.

choices.text: Writing long prompts
choices.why: Length is not a goal. Each line has to earn its place against the test.

choices.text: A test that says whether a goal was met
choices.why: Yes. Without a test, a change cannot be told from an improvement.

choices.text: Using the newest and largest model
choices.why: A bigger model is a different input to the same cycle, not the cycle.

prompt: In the measured run, how many of `v3`'s twenty replies contained `seven`?
hint: Read the last line of the loop's output.

prompt: Four draws from `v2` gave `seven` three times. Why was that not enough to keep `v2`?

choices.text: Four replies are an impression; over twenty it missed eight times
choices.why: Right. The count over twenty showed what four could not, and `v3` passed sixteen.

choices.text: Three out of four is below the 80% that a prompt must reach
choices.why: No such threshold was set. The point is that four runs measure too little.

choices.text: `v2` was never tested at all, so its result could not be trusted
choices.why: It was tested, twice: four draws, then twenty.

choices.text: The fourth draw changed the model
choices.why: Draws do not change the model. They differ because each uses a different seed.

prompt: `v2` added `at` after `answer :` and still gave `six` sometimes. What does that say about the fix?
hint: What could the model see after `: at`?

choices.text: It made things worse than `v1`
choices.why: `v1` passed once in twenty and `v2` twelve times. It was a real improvement.

choices.text: `six` is correct for some days of the week
choices.why: The goal said the weekday opening time, which is `seven`. `six` is a closing time.

choices.text: The word `at` should never appear inside a prompt
choices.why: The word helped. It was not enough on its own.

choices.text: It fixed the form of the reply, a time, but not which time
choices.why: Yes. After `: at` the model cannot tell an opening question from a closing one, so `seven` and `six` tie.

prompt: Why are the versions kept in files such as `prompts/v2.txt`?
hint: What would be lost without them?

choices.text: Because `toylm` can only read prompts from files
choices.why: `toylm` takes the prompt on the command line; the files are for the person.

choices.text: So the model can learn from earlier versions of its prompt
choices.why: The model sees only the text it is given now.

choices.text: Prompts in files run faster than prompts that are typed in
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: So a regression can be traced to a version
choices.why: Right. Versioning lets you compare, go back, and find the change that broke something.

prompt: The specific prompt for the door notice has four parts. Which of these lines are output format? Choose all that apply.
hint: Which lines say what the reply must look like, rather than what it is about?

choices.text: Write the notice in English
choices.why: Yes: the language of the reply is part of its format.

choices.text: at most four lines, one line per rule
choices.why: Yes: length and layout are format.

choices.text: Opening hours: Monday to Saturday 07:00 to 18:00
choices.why: That is input data, the facts the reply must be right about.

choices.text: You are writing the notice for the door of Café Aurora
choices.why: That is the instruction and context: the task and where it is going.

prompt: A colleague's prompt says only `Summarise this complaint.` The summaries are correct and the support team cannot use them. Which part is most likely missing?
hint: The table names what goes wrong without each part.

choices.text: Input data
choices.why: The complaint is there; the summaries are correct.

choices.text: Output format
choices.why: Yes: a reply that is correct and cannot be used where it is going is what a missing format looks like.

choices.text: Instruction
choices.why: There is one, and the model followed it.

choices.text: Context about which model is being used
choices.why: The model does not need to be told what it is. The team needs a shape it can use.

prompt: Put the prompt engineering cycle in order.
hint: It begins before any prompt is written.
items: State the goal in one sentence
Write test inputs with what a good reply must contain
Change one thing in the prompt and save it as a new version
Run every version against the same tests and count the passes

prompt: A teammate shows you one excellent reply and says the new prompt is better. What is the right next step?
hint: What did the twenty-run test add?

choices.text: Run both prompts on the same tests, many times, and compare counts
choices.why: Right. One reply is an impression; the count over many runs is the measurement.

choices.text: Accept it; an excellent reply proves the prompt works
choices.why: One reply cannot show how often the prompt fails.

choices.text: Ask the model which of the two prompts it prefers
choices.why: The model's preference is another generated text, not a measurement.

choices.text: Make the prompt longer, since a longer prompt carries more parts
choices.why: Longer is not better on its own. Test first.

prompt: Which statement about a chat request is true?
hint: Think about what is text and what is not.

choices.text: The model checks that the assistant turns were really written by itself
choices.why: There is no such check. They are text in a list.

choices.text: The system message is hidden from the model as well as from the user
choices.why: The user does not see it. The model does: it is part of the text.

choices.text: A conversation must alternate user and assistant, or the model refuses
choices.why: The model continues whatever text it gets.

choices.text: Earlier assistant turns are text that any program is free to write
choices.why: Yes. Nothing marks them as the model's own, so the model cannot tell who wrote them.
